questions.q: What core idea does Oracle center its performance tuning methodology on, per this lesson?
options: DB Time — the total time the database spent on user work, split into CPU time and wait time
The buffer cache hit ratio, pushed toward 99% or higher
The number of tables in the database
The version number of the Oracle instance
questions.explain: Oracle's time model accounts for all database time as either CPU time or a specific named wait event, summed as DB Time.

questions.q: What is a 'wait event' in Oracle?
options: A named reason a session was waiting instead of running, such as db file sequential read
A scheduled job that runs at a fixed time
An error raised when a query times out
A type of Oracle index
questions.explain: Wait events are specific, named reasons for session waits, visible in views like V$SESSION and V$ACTIVE_SESSION_HISTORY.

questions.q: Why did Oracle move away from ratio-based tuning (like chasing a high buffer cache hit ratio) as a primary methodology?
options: Because DB Time and wait events give a direct, evidence-based answer to where time is actually going, rather than an indirect proxy
Because ratios are no longer calculable in modern Oracle versions
Because SQL Server also abandoned ratio-based tuning
Because ratios only apply to MySQL
questions.explain: The wait interface and DB Time model let a DBA see exactly where time goes, instead of inferring health from an indirect ratio.

questions.q: What does ADDM (Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor) do?
options: Runs automatically after every AWR snapshot and produces ranked findings and recommendations based on time model data
Automatically rewrites slow SQL statements without DBA review
Replaces the need to ever gather optimizer statistics
Is a SQL Server tool with no Oracle equivalent
questions.explain: ADDM analyzes AWR data automatically and ranks findings by DB Time impact, but its recommendations still need verification.

questions.q: In the measure → identify → change → verify loop applied to Oracle, what should happen at the 'change' step?
options: Make exactly one change, not several at once, so its effect can be isolated
Apply every plausible fix simultaneously to save time
Skip straight to verify without making any change
Only ever change initialization parameters, never SQL or indexes
questions.explain: Making one change at a time preserves the ability to verify what actually caused an improvement — the same discipline from SQL Server tuning.
